or Twi, is the language prevalent in the Gold Coast countries between the rivers Asini and Tanno on the W. and the Volta on the E., and extends even beyond this river; its southern boundary is the sea-coast, while the upper course of the Volta, and the Kong mountains are its northern limits.

or Akan, probably meaning 'foremost; genuine'; from kaŋ, first; e.g. ɔyɛ Ɔkanni, he is a born or genuine Tshi man. 'Akan' is used in a wider sense (a) for the dialects of Akem, Asante, Adanse &c. (s. § 2), and (b) in a narrower for those of Akem and Asante only.

The name 'Twi' being used not only by the natives themselves, but also by the Accras and tribes to the east of the Volta, (in the form 'Otshui'), it has been retained as the generic appellation of the language.

The dialect is considered to be spoken purest (a) in Akem; but by its "dainty and affected mode of expression" (e. g. the frequent ɛ & ɔ, where most other dialects have simply e & o, as, ades, ases, kɔree, ɔbɔɔ, sɔɔ, = ade, ase, kɔe, ɔbo, so), it appears less suited to become the common dialect of all-Tshi tribes.

The dialect of Asante agrees in all essentials with that of Akem, only the pronunciation is "broad and hard (tɛtɛrɛ denneenɛŋ)", e. g. people say "kērɛ" instead of "kyerɛ", - whilst in Akem it is "soft and delicate (bɔkɔɔ freŋkyemm)".

The dialect of Akuapem, derived from Akem and Akwam (an Akan dialect of old standing) and having points of contact with Brɔŋ and Fante, became about 1842 the literary form intelligible to all the other.

The name applied by the Asantes to a group of dialects (also known as Kāmănă) spoken in the districts N. & N. E. of the Akan districts, including Okwawu, Dkorănsă, and others, which are considered genuine Tshi but may contain foreign elements.
A dialect spoken in the districts N. & N. E. of the Akan districts, also known as Brɔŋ, which does not differ much from genuine Tshi.

A branch of the Akan language spoken by several maritime tribes in the South, which differs from other dialects by changing initial sounds (kw, gw, hw) before palatal vowels and by curtailing final vowels.
A language belonging to the Kwa group, spoken in the area between Senegal and Eastern Nigeria, specifically within the Ewe-Tshi subgroup, encompassing the Akan-Fante dialects.

pl. a-, witch, hag; wizard, sorcerer. pr. 59-62. 139. 2154; cf. bayi, ayɛŋ, baninyɛŋ, baayɛŋ, ɔbonsam, kabere. The natives describe a wizard or witch as a man or woman who stands in some agreement with the devil. At night, when all are asleep, he (or she) rises or rather leaves his (her) body, as a snake casts its slough, and goes out emitting flames from his eyes, nose, mouth, ears, armpits; he may walk with his head on the ground and his feet up; he catches and eats animals, or kills men either by drinking their blood or by catching their soul,-which he boils and eats, where-upon the person dies; or he bites them that they become full of sores. Some change themselves into leopards, snakes, antelopes; some apply their witchcraft also to trade when selling things.
